title: What it costs in life
hookLine: Thoreau: the cost of a thing is the amount of life exchanged for it (Walden 1)

cards: A new pair of shoes, and a price on the tag. Is that what they cost? Henry David Thoreau would ask how many hours of your life they took.
At the start of Walden, his book about living by a pond in the Massachusetts woods, Thoreau sits down to do some accounts. Not just in money, though he lists that too, down to the nails.
He writes a sentence that turns every price tag around: "the cost of a thing is the amount of what I will call life which is required to be exchanged for it, immediately or in the long run."
Today's word is his book: Walden.

teach.b: First, the word he chooses. Not money, not effort: life. A dollar stands in for the hours spent earning it, hours that don't come back.

teach.h: NOW, OR IN THE LONG RUN.
teach.b: Second, the long run. Some things cost life up front. Others cost it slowly: the bigger house that needs the longer commute, the payments that keep you at a job you'd leave.
Thoreau wants both counted. Third, a story he tells to make the point. Thoreau imagines racing a friend to a town some distance away.
The friend will work for the train fare, then ride. Thoreau will set out on foot right now.

He says, in paraphrase, that he'll get there first, because by the time the friend has earned the fare, the walker has already arrived. It's a joke, and it isn't. The train looks faster until you price it in life.
Fourth, what he does not say. Thoreau isn't telling everyone to move to a cabin; he says plainly in Walden that he doesn't want anyone to adopt his way of living.
His point is the arithmetic, done honestly, by each person, and the sum can come out either way. Some things are worth every hour they cost: a tool that lasts, a trip to see someone you love, a gift.
Thoreau's ledger doesn't forbid spending life. It asks that the spending be chosen, with the hours counted, rather than slipping away while nobody looks at the bill.

how: Readers of Walden, including people interested in simple living, quote Thoreau's measure of cost in life when weighing purchases, jobs and the hours they ask for.

games.q: you and a friend both want to reach a town some distance away. your friend will work to earn the train fare, then ride. what does Thoreau choose?
o: work alongside the friend and ride too.
set out on foot right now.
stay home; it isn't worth the trip.
games.why: Thoreau walks, and says he'll arrive first: by the time the fare is earned, the walker is already there.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you bought recently, or are thinking of buying, and gently do Thoreau's sum: roughly how many hours of work did it take, or will it take?
Hold that number beside the thing itself without judging; maybe it's worth every hour, maybe not. If you pray, you can bring the question into your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Walden. Thoreau's book about living by a pond, where he measures the cost of a thing in the life it takes to earn it. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: chosen, with the hours counted. Every price is paid in life. See you tomorrow.
